To choose the first artificial intelligence tool, the control rule comes before the choice of software. According to Insee, in October 2026, 12.5% of records are reworked. This finding shifts the decision: management needs to explain the approval criteria before comparing the features offered by software publishers.

## The reported delay conceals the work of correction

According to Insee, in October 2026, 12.5% of records are reworked. The result separates production speed from the time required for approval. A record sent faster can still wait for a review, a missing document or an authorisation. Measurement therefore includes the handover between people and correction of the result. The first tool cannot be selected from the number of tasks processed alone. Management compares a complete result, including rework, with the method already used. This boundary defines what is actually measured and prevents activity from being confused with completed work.

The measurement published by Insee in October 2026 covers 10,000 records. That detail matters as much as the reported outcome: a sample describes a task and its conditions, rather than every organisation. A comparison must retain the same approval criteria, documents and exceptions. Changing these elements changes the meaning of the result. The process owner keeps the definition of what is accepted and what requires correction. That record makes it possible to return to the observed case whenever software produces an answer whose basis remains uncertain or insufficiently documented.

The CNIL measurement in September 2026, records 24 hours of control. The delay refers to an identified stage and does not imply that every verification is unnecessary. A check can prevent an unsupported decision while still requiring a simpler organisation. Management separates review time, waiting time and correction time. It can then identify a missing rule, a late document or a responsibility that remains shared. The work done by software becomes observable through these handovers rather than through a general promise of speed. The distinction gives the decision a documented basis.

According to Banque de France, in August 2026, processing takes 36 hours. That duration can only be compared with the previous control after examining the scope: the publications do not necessarily describe the same record. Placing figures together does not prove an improvement. Management asks for the definition of each measurement before selecting a target. The same label can cover data entry, a decision or completion of a request. Making that difference visible prevents a transfer of work to another team from being presented as an overall improvement in the process.

## The control rule comes before the software choice

The distinction made by Insee leads to defining a completed record before choosing software. The process owner writes down the elements required for a decision and identifies the person who can approve it. This rule remains readable by someone unfamiliar with the program. Exceptions retain their reasons so that a tool defect can be distinguished from disagreement over the expected result. The trial can then compare software output with this definition. This organisation does not presume success; it gives the comparison a stable meaning and makes a refusal to deploy understandable.

Under the control described by CNIL, there is another boundary on the decision: approval must remain assigned. A plausible result may be incomplete without being obviously false. The record therefore keeps the documents used and the reason for the decision. The owner can check what is missing without reconstructing all the work. The rule is not to multiply stages but to define the evidence required at the handover that commits the organisation. When this evidence is missing, the record remains pending. Software is not given the power to turn the absence of an answer into implicit permission.

## The next review examines completed work

Reading Banque de France suggests a question for the next process review: which stage remains included in the reported delay? The answer can be checked against the documents, decisions and corrections in the record. The owner retains an accepted example and a rejected example so that the rule can be explained without a sales demonstration. A person is also assigned to arbitrate a new case. This check makes the work remaining after software output visible and gives management a specific reason to continue or stop the trial. That reason can be inspected by the people affected.

The scope used by Insee finally recalls that repeating a figure does not replace observing a task. Before extending the result, management examines corrected records and the conditions under which control took place. It retains the possibility of returning to the previous method if the result can no longer be explained. The decision then depends neither on the novelty of the product nor on the volume of answers displayed. It depends on a result accepted under a known rule. The rule drawn from this reading of Insee is simple: choose the tool after defining completed work.
